candidate_relations.reason: Absent cold and electric responses indicate nonvital pulp rather than pulpitis, while percussion tenderness and apical radiolucency localize disease periapically.
No response to vitality testing supports pulpal necrosis, which can cause the apical inflammation but is not the symptomatic apical diagnosis requested.
CBCT demonstrates a C-shaped palatal canal, but this anatomic variant is a treatment-relevant feature rather than the painful apical lesion.
A periapical radiolucency alone cannot establish a cyst, and no histology or well-corticated cystic characterization is supplied.
Pain during prior therapy and residual coronal filling material motivate retreatment, but treatment failure does not specify the percussion-sensitive apical periodontal inflammation.

Two palatal orifices joining into a C-shaped ribbon can be overlooked during treatment, but the record does not prove a missed or false canal and this would be an etiology rather than the apical diagnosis.
Axial and sagittal CBCT confirm two palatal canals joining in a C-shaped configuration, which is anatomy accompanying rather than replacing symptomatic apical periodontitis.
Temporary sealing and incomplete coronal filling indicate problematic root-canal therapy, but the label does not identify the diseased apical periodontal tissue.
Periapical radiolucency at the distobuccal root and percussion tenderness support periapical periodontitis, but the candidate does not explicitly preserve the symptomatic state.
Negative thermal and electric tests are consistent with a necrotic pulp, which is upstream of but not equivalent to the symptomatic apical periodontal lesion.
The ribbon-like union of two palatal canals is a C-shaped morphology relevant to retreatment, not the diagnosis producing apical percussion pain.
Spontaneous dull pain and percussion tenderness establish active symptoms, so an unqualified chronic apical periodontitis label conflicts with the stated symptomatic state.
Apical periodontitis correctly localizes the radiolucent percussion-sensitive process but omits that it is symptomatic in tooth 17.
